meaning_en: the series of stages a living thing passes through
scene: {A} draws a frog's whole life on one wall. {B} adds a tiny tadpole wearing a graduation cap.
bubble: {B} finished the life cycle with style!
example: Our science project shows the life cycle of a butterfly.

options: Mia drew the life cycle of a bee, from egg to adult.
My grandfather told us his life cycle: he was born in Cusco and became a teacher.
She enjoys a healthy life cycle of eating well and exercising.
practice.why: A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through.

meaning_en: to remain united with other people
scene: {A} and {B} are stuck in a lift full of jelly. They hold hands and refuse to let go.
bubble: We stick together, even in jelly!
example: If we stick together, the group project will be easy.

options: The students stuck together their answers after the test to compare marks.
He stuck together at his desk all evening to finish the report.
The team stuck together when the match got difficult.
practice.why: Stick together means to stay united, not to glue paper.

meaning_en: to skip the introduction and say the main point
scene: {A} gives a ten-minute speech about lunch. {B} holds up a sign: 'Just say pizza.'
bubble: Let's cut to the chase: pizza!
example: Let's cut to the chase: can you lend me the money?

options: They cut to the chase by taking a shortcut through the park.
She cut to the chase and asked for a raise.
He cut to the chase and told the long story from the beginning.
practice.why: Cut to the chase means go straight to the main point.

meaning_en: the arguments for and against a decision
scene: {A} weighs a puppy on one side of a scale and a sofa on the other. {B} takes notes.
bubble: The pros and cons of a pet sofa!
example: We listed the pros and cons before buying a flat.

options: The teacher announced the pros and cons of the exam: seventy students passed and ten failed.
The pros and cons of the train were the first and last carriages.
Before moving abroad, they talked about the pros and cons.
practice.why: The pros and cons are the good and bad sides of a choice.

meaning_en: to sell your home or your business and move away
scene: {A} puts a 'for sale' sign on a house and a goldfish bowl. {B} cries and packs socks.
bubble: {A} sold up and left with a goldfish!
example: After forty years, the baker sold up and moved to the coast.

options: When prices fell, many farmers sold up.
The shop sold up all its stock in the first hour of the sale.
She sold up her old bike to a neighbour for twenty pounds.
practice.why: Sell up means to sell all you own, such as a home or business.

text: you need money to make money
meaning_en: used to say that starting a business needs capital
meaning_es: para ganar dinero hay que tenerlo
scene: {A} gets a piggy bank for a gift. {B} whispers, 'It works better if you put money in it.'
bubble: You need money to make money, {A}!
example: He bought a second shop with profits, because you need money to make money.

options: Anyone can win the lottery, so you need money to make money.
Starting a company costs a lot: you need money to make money.
You need money to make money, so you must always be honest with friends.
practice.why: It means starting a business needs capital first.

meaning_en: to finish something in a satisfying way
scene: {A} finishes a long talk by juggling three oranges. {B} claps and throws a banana.
bubble: {A} rounded off the show perfectly!
example: We rounded off the evening with ice cream and a song.

options: He rounded off his homework before he had even opened the book.
The film started well but was rounded off in the middle.
The trip was rounded off with a visit to the old castle.
practice.why: Round off means to end something in a nice, satisfying way.

meaning_en: to tell the authorities about something wrong inside an organization
scene: {A} sees a sandwich thief in the school kitchen. {B} blows a whistle so loudly the hens wake up.
bubble: {B} blew the whistle on the sandwich thief!
example: The clerk blew the whistle on the unsafe factory.

options: He blew the whistle on his sister's present by telling her about it.
She blew the whistle when she saw the company cheating customers.
The manager blew the whistle on the meeting and everyone went home.
practice.why: To blow the whistle is to report bad behaviour to the authorities.

meaning_en: to make progress early or faster than others
scene: {A} runs out of bed first and reaches the cake before seven o'clock. {B} is still asleep.
bubble: {A} got ahead of the whole family!
example: To get ahead in this job, you should learn a second language.

options: She worked hard on weekends to get ahead of the other students.
He got ahead of the bus stop and waited for his friend.
She got ahead with her cold after resting in bed.
practice.why: Get ahead means to do better or progress faster than others.

meaning_en: to deal with something step by step until it is finished
scene: {A} faces a mountain of homework. {B} hands over a spoon and says, 'One bite at a time.'
bubble: {B} worked through it, one bite at a time.
example: We worked through the problem together until it made sense.

options: The tourists worked through the museum in five minutes, so they saw almost nothing.
It took the team an hour to work through all the emails.
The factory worked through three new machines last year.
practice.why: Work through means deal with something step by step.

meaning_en: to return something to where it belongs
scene: {A} puts away a pair of shoes. They run back out the door. {B} sighs and chases them.
bubble: {B} cannot put away these naughty shoes!
example: Please put away your toys before dinner.

options: After the picnic, we put away the plates and cups.
The dentist put away my toothache with an injection.
I put away my homework to ask for help.
practice.why: Put away means to return something to its proper place.

meaning_en: to just manage to cope with work or money
scene: {A} swims in a pool of bills and emails. {B} throws a rubber duck as a lifebuoy.
bubble: {A} is keeping their head above water!
example: With two jobs and a baby, she is just keeping her head above water.

options: She kept her head above water when she won the school prize easily.
He kept his head above water and became the richest man in town.
Many small shops are struggling to keep their heads above water.
practice.why: It means to cope, usually with money or work, but only just.

meaning_en: used to ask somebody to help you
scene: {A} carries a giant pile of books. {B} holds out a hand, then a hand-shaped cake.
bubble: Give me a hand, {B}, please!
example: Could you give me a hand with this heavy box?

options: My uncle gave me a hand for my birthday, a new bike.
He gave me a hand with my maths homework.
Please give me a hand; I want to be left alone.
practice.why: Give me a hand is an informal way to ask for help.

meaning_en: to accept a difficult fact after some time
scene: {A} cannot believe the zoo has closed. {B} brings tea and a big hug.
bubble: {A} is coming to terms with it.
example: It took him months to come to terms with the loss of his job.

options: He came to terms with his cousin at the airport and hugged him.
She came to terms with her homework and got ten out of ten.
She is coming to terms with the idea of moving house.
practice.why: Come to terms with means to accept something difficult.

meaning_en: to realize that somebody is trying to trick you
scene: {A} dresses as a banker and asks for a free pizza. {B} sees through the moustache at once.
bubble: {B} saw through {A} in a second!
example: I saw through his excuse straight away.

options: The teacher saw through our plan to skip the quiz.
We saw through the match on TV and cheered for our team.
He saw through his friend's good news and gave him a big hug.
practice.why: See through means to understand someone's trick.

meaning_en: lasting as much time as is needed
scene: {A} sets a timer for the pasta. {B} waits until the pasta is cooked long enough.
bubble: Cook it long enough, {B}!
example: Boil the pasta long enough or it will be hard.

options: She is long enough to reach the top shelf.
He waited long enough and left the cinema after one minute.
We did not wait long enough, so the cake was still raw.
practice.why: Long enough means for as much time as is needed.

meaning_en: to laugh at somebody in an unkind way
scene: {A} wears a sock on each ear. {B} laughs so hard a rubber duck flies out of their pocket.
bubble: Please do not make fun of {A}!
example: It is not kind to make fun of other people's accents.

options: They made fun of his hat, and he felt sad.
We made fun of the picnic and ate sandwiches in the park.
He made fun of the holiday he spent by the sea and loved every day.
practice.why: Make fun of means to laugh at someone in an unkind way.

meaning_en: to suddenly become too frightened to do something
scene: {A} climbs to the top diving board. {B} watches {A}'s knees shake and slowly step back.
bubble: {A} lost their nerve at the top!
example: She lost her nerve and did not sing on stage.

options: She lost her nerve and shouted at the waiter.
He nearly asked her out, but lost his nerve.
I lost my nerve and could not find my keys.
practice.why: Lose your nerve means to become too scared to do something.

meaning_en: to invent something clever or unusual in your mind
scene: {A} thinks up a flying bicycle made of spaghetti. {B} tests it and flies upside down.
bubble: {A} thought up the silliest idea ever!
example: She thought up a clever way to save water.

options: Can you think up a name for our new puppy?
He thought up his grandfather as he looked at the old photo.
I thought up at the exam question for ten minutes before writing.
practice.why: Think up means to invent an idea in your mind.

meaning_en: to make something start
scene: {A} spins a giant ball down a hill. {B} yells, 'The meeting has started!'
bubble: {B} got the ball rolling by yelling!
example: To get the ball rolling, I will make the first speech.

options: He got the ball rolling when he finished the race in first place.
They got the ball rolling and ended the project last week.
Let's get the ball rolling with a short quiz.
practice.why: Get the ball rolling means to start something.

meaning_en: to be careful because there is a danger
scene: {A} walks along a path full of banana skins. {B} shouts and jumps on a skateboard.
bubble: Watch out, {A}! Banana skins!
example: Watch out! There's a car coming round the corner.

options: Watch out the match on Saturday with me.
Watch out for ice on the road tonight.
I watched out the shop for an hour before it opened.
practice.why: Watch out is a warning to be careful.

meaning_en: very nearly all of a group
scene: {A} counts: nine hundred cats love fish, one cat loves broccoli. {B} points at the broccoli cat.
bubble: The vast majority love fish, not broccoli!
example: The vast majority of students passed the exam.

options: There was a vast majority of snow on the roof last night.
A vast majority of people in the room said no and one said yes, so the plan passed.
A vast majority of people prefer summer to winter.
practice.why: The vast majority means nearly all of a group.

meaning_en: to delay progress
scene: {A} builds a sandcastle for hours. A wave sets {A} back. {B} offers a bucket.
bubble: {A} was set back by one cheeky wave!
example: The storm set back the building work by two weeks.

options: The bad news set the project back a month.
She set back her bike in the garage after school.
The dentist set back my tooth and it stopped hurting.
practice.why: Set back means to delay progress.

meaning_en: one small part at a time
scene: {A} eats a whole elephant-shaped cake. {B} says, 'Bit by bit, please.'
bubble: Bit by bit, {A} cleaned the plate!
example: Bit by bit, he learned to speak English.

options: The boy was bit by bit by a mosquito last night.
She saved bit by bit and bought a bike.
I want bit by bit more cheese on my pizza.
practice.why: Bit by bit means one small part at a time.

meaning_en: to fail to happen after being planned
scene: {A} and {B} plan a picnic. The sandwiches grow legs and walk away. The plan falls through.
bubble: Our picnic fell through. Literally!
example: Our holiday fell through because the hotel closed.

options: The deal fell through at the last minute.
My friend fell through his exam, so he studied more.
The two sisters fell through after an argument about the TV.
practice.why: Fall through means a plan fails to happen.

meaning_en: to look at a whole text from start to end
scene: {A} reads a sandwich recipe aloud. {B} reads the whole book through from page one to the end.
bubble: {B} read through the entire menu!
example: Please read through the instructions before you start.

options: She read through his face that he was angry.
He read through his notes on the train.
The librarian read through the book from the shelf and put it on the table.
practice.why: Read through means to look at all of a text from start to end.

text: strike while the iron is hot
meaning_en: to act while the chance is still there
scene: {A} grabs a hot pan and starts the pancakes. {B} yells, 'Strike now, flip later!'
bubble: {A} struck while the iron was hot!
example: She applied the day the job was advertised, striking while the iron was hot.

options: She struck while the iron was hot and left the party early.
He struck while the iron was hot, so he waited another year.
Strike while the iron is hot: ask her now.
practice.why: It means to act while the chance is there.

meaning_en: said in private and not to be reported
scene: {A} whispers a secret to {B} behind a plant. A parrot repeats it. 'Off the record!' shouts {B}.
bubble: Off the record, the parrot knows everything!
example: Off the record, I think the manager will leave.

options: The singer's new song was sold off the record in the shop.
He told me off the record that prices will rise.
He told everyone off the record, on the school radio and online.
practice.why: Off the record means said in private, not to be reported.

meaning_en: to print or copy a number of pages quickly
scene: {A} presses a button and the photocopier runs off a hundred cats. {B} is amazed.
bubble: {A} ran off a hundred cat pictures!
example: Can you run off twenty copies of this page, please?

options: The teacher ran off the worksheets before class.
He ran off a bad cold by resting for two days.
The shop ran off milk, so we went to another one.
practice.why: Run off here means to print or copy pages quickly.

meaning_en: to stop eating or doing something, or to remove by cutting
scene: {A} cuts out sweets and cakes. {B} secretly hides a chocolate biscuit in each pocket.
bubble: {A} cut out sugar, but {B} did not!
example: My doctor told me to cut out salt.

options: He cut out the car when the road became busy.
The tailor cut out his friends for the party.
He cut out the article from the newspaper.
practice.why: Cut out means stop eating or doing something, or remove with scissors.

meaning_en: the nervous feeling you get before something important
scene: {A} must sing in front of the school. {B} offers a butterfly net for the nerves.
bubble: {A} has butterflies in the stomach!
example: I always get butterflies in my stomach before a match.

options: She had butterflies in her stomach on her first day at school.
I had butterflies in my stomach after eating a huge pizza.
He had butterflies in his stomach when he was bored at the cinema.
practice.why: It means the nervous feeling before something important.

meaning_en: to make something last longer than necessary
scene: {A} tells a story about toast that lasts all afternoon. {B} tries to hold the clock still.
bubble: {A} drew out the story of toast!
example: The lawyers drew out the meeting to avoid a decision.

options: They drew out the match by scoring early.
The teacher drew out the lesson to finish it quickly.
She drew out the joke until nobody laughed.
practice.why: Draw out means to make something last longer than needed.

meaning_en: for the same reason, applied to another case
scene: {A} says dogs should be allowed in class. {B} adds, 'By the same token, cats too!'
bubble: By the same token, fish need desks!
example: If we let him leave early, by the same token we must let her go.

options: By the same token, we missed the bus, so we took a taxi.
By the same token, they should pay everyone the same.
He lost his ticket; by the same token, he enjoyed the film.
practice.why: By the same token means for the same reason, in another case.

meaning_en: in private, where the public does not see the work
scene: {A} lifts the curtain: a giant cat and ten monkeys are making the show work. {B} gasps.
bubble: {B} saw what happens behind the scenes!
example: The director spent months working behind the scenes.

options: The tourists enjoyed the view behind the scenes from the hotel window.
He sat behind the scenes in the cinema and watched the film.
Teachers do a lot of work behind the scenes before a school play.
practice.why: Behind the scenes means in private, where the public does not see.

meaning_en: to do your fair share of the work
scene: {A} lies in a hammock while {B} cleans the whole kitchen. A cat looks at {A} with disapproval.
bubble: {A}, please pull your weight!
example: Everyone in the team must pull their weight.

options: He never pulls his weight at home, so his sister does everything.
She pulled her weight and lost five kilos.
The class pulled their weight by buying the teacher a present.
practice.why: Pull your weight means do your fair share of work.

meaning_en: to end up fine after a difficult change
scene: {A} falls off a ladder and lands on a pile of pillows. {B} claps and hands over a trophy.
bubble: {A} landed on their feet. Perfect!
example: After losing his job, he landed on his feet with a better one.

options: After the long journey, we landed on our feet at the hotel.
She always lands on her feet, whatever happens.
He landed on his feet in the exam, so he failed.
practice.why: Land on your feet means to end up well after a problem.

meaning_en: used to add a surprising or exact detail
scene: {A} says, 'I never go swimming.' {B} points at a medal. 'As a matter of fact, you are champion.'
bubble: As a matter of fact, {A} won gold!
example: As a matter of fact, I have met the Queen.

options: I did not mind. As a matter of fact, I enjoyed the long walk.
She asked me, as a matter of fact, to open the window.
He likes cheese. As a matter of fact, he hates it.
practice.why: It adds a surprising or exact detail to what you said.

meaning_en: to be the opposite of what is expected or accepted
scene: {A} wears a swimsuit in the snow. {B} says, 'That flies in the face of common sense!'
bubble: {A} flies in the face of common sense!
example: The new law flies in the face of what most people want.

options: The pilot flew in the face of the storm and landed safely.
His idea flies in the face of all the evidence.
He flew in the face of his sister to get to the party early.
practice.why: Fly in the face of means to go against what is expected.

meaning_en: to save something for later
scene: {A} puts aside one chocolate from each box. {B} finds a mountain of them for a rainy day.
bubble: {A} put aside chocolate for later!
example: I put aside some money every month for holidays.

options: She put aside the cup after dinner and washed it.
I put aside the window to let in fresh air.
She put aside the book to talk to me.
practice.why: Put aside means to save something for later.

meaning_en: to look at or explain something again carefully
scene: {A} explains the rules of the board game. Again. {B} yawns, then goes over them with a drum.
bubble: {B} goes over the rules for the third time!
example: Let's go over the plan once more before we leave.

options: The teacher went over the homework with us.
The soup went over the cooker when I was not watching.
He went over his grandmother's house by bike and arrived late.
practice.why: Go over means to explain or check something again.

meaning_en: to keep contacting somebody after you separate
scene: {A} and {B} wave from a plane and a train while sending a hundred postcards.
bubble: Stay in touch, {B}! Send pizza!
example: We moved to different cities but stayed in touch by email.

options: I stayed in touch with the cold and rested at home.
Please stay in touch while you are abroad.
We stayed in touch at the bus stop for an hour.
practice.why: Stay in touch means to keep contact with someone.

meaning_en: to help somebody, especially in a difficult moment
scene: {A} is carrying a lorry full of lemons. {B} helps out with a very small spoon.
bubble: {B} helped out. Very slowly.
example: Neighbours helped out after the flood.

options: The driver helped out the bus for the afternoon and went home.
She helped out the money to a friend who had none.
Can you help out at the school fair on Saturday?
practice.why: Help out means to give someone help, often in a hard moment.

meaning_en: to give someone a lower grade
scene: {A} writes 'Nice!' on {B}'s homework. The teacher marks it down and draws a sad cloud.
bubble: {B} was marked down for dancing in class!
example: The teacher marked me down for spelling mistakes.

options: The boy marked down the teacher for being late.
You will be marked down if you copy the answers.
I marked down the bus after the show.
practice.why: Mark down means to give a lower mark.

meaning_en: to happen during the period before an event
scene: {A} blows up a balloon each day. In the lead-up to the party, {B} hides the pin.
bubble: Everything led up to the big party!
example: The events leading up to the strike were strange.

options: The team leads up to the other team with two goals.
She led up to her speech by walking home.
There was a lot of excitement in the weeks leading up to the show.
practice.why: Lead up to means to happen in the time before an event.

meaning_en: the abilities you need to speak well in front of a group
scene: {A} gives a talk with a puppet and a tuba. {B} gives {A} ten out of ten for presentation skills.
bubble: Great presentation skills, {A}!
example: Good presentation skills will help you in any job.

options: She took a course to improve her presentation skills.
Presentation skills are the gifts you receive at a party.
He has excellent presentation skills, so he often writes long essays.
practice.why: Presentation skills are the abilities needed to speak well to a group.

meaning_en: to think about something that happened in the past
scene: {A} reads an old diary and laughs at a photo from 1999. {B} looks back with a funny hat.
bubble: Looking back, {A} loved that hat.
example: Looking back, I should have studied more.

options: She looked back for her glasses and found them under the bed.
She looked back at her school days with a smile.
I looked back my sister while Mum was at work.
practice.why: Look back means to think about the past.

meaning_en: to make a small mistake
scene: {A} types a very serious email and writes 'Dear Pizza' instead of 'Dear Peter'. {B} spots the slip-up.
bubble: {A} slipped up. Dear Pizza!
example: Everyone slips up sometimes, so do not worry.

options: The bank slipped up and sent two letters to the wrong house.
I slipped up a sweater and went out into the cold.
She slipped up the answer in the margin.
practice.why: Slip up means to make a small mistake.

meaning_en: to try to make people admire you
scene: {A} drives a golden skateboard through the canteen. {B} tells them, 'Stop showing off!'
bubble: {A} is showing off with a golden board!
example: He likes to show off his new trainers.

options: The guide showed off the visitors around the old castle.
He showed off the film at the cinema last night.
She showed off her piano skills at the party.
practice.why: Show off means to try to make people admire you.

meaning_en: to destroy a building on purpose
scene: {A} watches a crane pull down an old school. {B} cries because the swings were there.
bubble: They pulled down the school. {B} waves goodbye.
example: They plan to pull down the old cinema next year.

options: The council pulled down the empty factory.
She pulled down the hill on her bike to reach the village.
The wind pulled down my enthusiasm.
practice.why: Pull down means to destroy a building on purpose.

meaning_en: very common and therefore not valuable
scene: {A} holds a toy robot. {B} opens a cupboard with a hundred identical toy robots.
bubble: Robots are a dime a dozen here!
example: Cheap phone covers are a dime a dozen at the market.

options: Their shop sold a dime a dozen of eggs on Sunday.
Rare coins are a dime a dozen, so collectors pay a fortune.
Good ideas are not a dime a dozen, so protect them.
practice.why: It means very common, so not valuable.

meaning_en: to end without causing any serious harm
scene: {A} says something silly at dinner. {B} hides under the table. By dessert it has all blown over.
bubble: It blew over before dessert!
example: Don't worry: the argument will blow over by tomorrow.

options: The news blew over the school, and everyone talked about it for weeks.
The storm blew over and we went back outside.
He blew over the candles on his cake and made a wish.
practice.why: Blow over means to end without causing serious harm.

meaning_en: to lead or manage a team or group
scene: {A} wears a captain's hat and heads up the school's cat-fashion committee. {B} is the only member.
bubble: {A} heads up the cat-fashion team!
example: She was chosen to head up the new design team.

options: The footballer headed up the ball into the net.
I headed up my emails before lunch.
Who will head up the project when the manager leaves?
practice.why: Head up means to lead a team or group.

meaning_en: to plan something in detail
scene: {A} maps out the whole summer on a giant poster. {B} asks, 'Where is the nap time?'
bubble: {A} mapped out the summer in colour!
example: We mapped out our route before the long trip.

options: She mapped out the town by taking a bus to the airport.
He mapped out a plan to save for a new bike.
He mapped out his homework by copying it from a friend.
practice.why: Map out means to plan something in detail.

meaning_en: to change your behaviour for the better
scene: {A} wakes up and tidies the room, brushes teeth and feeds the fish. {B} says, 'New leaf!'
bubble: {A} turned over a new leaf. Wow!
example: After the warning, he turned over a new leaf and arrived on time.

options: I'm going to turn over a new leaf and eat less sugar.
He turned over a new leaf and bought a new jacket.
She turned over a new leaf and moved to another flat.
practice.why: Turn over a new leaf means to start behaving better.

meaning_en: a lot of work or worries to deal with
scene: {A} balances twenty plates, a cat and a violin. {B} asks, 'Anything else on your plate?'
bubble: {A} has a lot on their plate!
example: I can't come tonight; I have a lot on my plate.

options: He has a lot on his plate because the cinema was full.
She has a lot on her plate, so she gets bored all day.
She has a lot on her plate with exams and a part-time job.
practice.why: It means a lot of work or worries to deal with.

meaning_en: to talk about ideas informally with other people
scene: {A} and {B} toss around ideas, and a pizza, over the kitchen table.
bubble: We tossed around ideas and a pizza!
example: The team tossed around a few ideas for the festival.

options: Let's toss around some names for the new club.
The coach tossed around the team before the match and won.
She tossed around her homework to the teacher.
practice.why: Toss around means to discuss ideas informally.

meaning_en: where nobody can see it
scene: {A} hides a chocolate bar where nobody can find it. {B}: 'Out of sight, out of mind... except my nose.'
bubble: Out of sight, but not out of {B}'s nose!
example: Keep the medicine out of sight of the children.

options: She is out of sight because she needs new glasses.
The ship sailed out of sight after a few minutes.
The dentist said my teeth were out of sight.
practice.why: Out of sight means where nobody can see it.

meaning_en: to make something easier to understand
scene: {A} switches on a huge torch in a dark cave. {B} says, 'Now that sheds light on the cave painting.'
bubble: {A} shed light on the cave mystery!
example: The report sheds light on why prices went up.

options: New research may shed light on this rare illness.
The teacher shed light on the lesson by turning it off.
He shed light on his coat when it got warm.
practice.why: Shed light on means to make something easier to understand.

meaning_en: to make a very big effort to achieve something
scene: {A} crosses a desert to buy {B} a birthday sandwich. {B} cries with joy.
bubble: {A} went to great lengths for a sandwich!
example: She went to great lengths to make the party perfect.

options: The film went to great lengths: it was three hours long.
He'd go to great lengths to win the game.
She goes to great lengths when she cuts her hair.
practice.why: Go to great lengths means to make a very big effort.

meaning_en: to refuse to accept or be involved with something
scene: {A} sees a mountain of homework and turns round, whistling. {B} says, 'You can't turn your back on this!'
bubble: {A} turned their back on the homework!
example: He turned his back on his old friends.

options: He turned his back on his sister's bag and carried it for her.

example: She left public life and moved to the country.

options: Public life is the life of animals in a zoo.
Public life can be very stressful.
Public life is the time you spend at home with your family.
practice.why: Public life is the part of life in politics or serving the community.

meaning_en: to make a place tidy by removing things you do not want
scene: {A} clears out the attic and finds a 1970s cheese, a ghost and a lot of old shoes. {B} runs.
bubble: {A} cleared out the attic. Surprise!
example: We cleared out the garage on Saturday.

options: She cleared out her wardrobe and gave the clothes away.
She cleared out the wardrobe by filling it with clothes.
He cleared out the room by putting all his things in it.
practice.why: Clear out means to tidy a place by removing what you do not want.

meaning_en: simple and unpolished, but good enough for now
scene: {A} builds a rough-and-ready bridge from two doors and a ladder. {B} crosses it with a goat.
bubble: A rough-and-ready bridge for a goat!
example: It was a rough-and-ready shelter, but it kept us dry.

options: It was a rough-and-ready table, but it was beautiful and perfect.
We made a rough-and-ready plan.
They made a rough-and-ready dessert, with no mistakes and a golden star.
practice.why: Rough and ready means simple and unpolished but good enough.

meaning_en: to continue with a plan or a rule without changing
scene: {A} wants to eat a different thing every day, but {B} sticks to the plan: pizza, pizza, pizza.
bubble: {B} stuck to the plan: pizza!
example: You must stick to the rules.

options: He stuck to the plan, then immediately changed it.
He stuck to the music and gave the plan to his sister.
She stuck to her plan despite the rain.
practice.why: Stick to means to continue with a plan or rule without changing.
